Big Data terminology

Definition

The collection, storage, and analysis of extremely large, complex, and often unstructured data sets that can be used by organizations to generate insights that would otherwise be impossible to make.

Source: Laney D (2001) 3-D Data Management: Controlling Data Volume, Velocity and Variety. Published by Meta Group.

INSY 2299 · Session 10
Business Intelligence

Data warehouse: where to store the data?

Data Warehouse

Set of databases designed to support decision making in an organization.

It is structured for fast online queries and exploration and may aggregate enormous amounts of data from many different operational systems.

Data Mart

Database or databases focused on addressing the concerns of a specific problem (subset of data warehouse: e.g., increasing customer retention, improving product quality) or business unit (e.g., marketing, finance or sales).

→ Both may contain huge volumes of data

Decision Support System (DSS)

Definition

A computer-based information system that is intended to support, but not replace, (managerial) decision makers in performing their problem-solving tasks.

DSS combine DATA, MODELS, and DISPLAYS to assist decision makers.

Idea: Combine the best features of human decision makers and computers.

INSY 2299 · Session 10
Analytics, AI and Machine Learning

Data mining: overview

Definition

Using computers to identify hidden patterns in large data sets and to build models from this data (data could be numeric, text as well as logs of web traffic).

Models used for

  • Customer segmentation and market basket analysis
  • Marketing and promotion targeting
  • Collaborative filtering and customer churn
  • Fraud detection, financial modeling, hiring and promotion

Prerequisites

  • Organization must have clean, consistent data
    – Wrong estimates from bad data leave firms grossly overexposed to risk
INSY 2299 · Session 10
Analytics, AI and Machine Learning

Data mining: examples

Customer segmentation—figuring out which customers are likely to be the most valuable to a firm.

Marketing and promotion targeting—identifying (predicting) which customers will respond to which offers at which price at what time.

Market basket analysis—determining which products customers buy together, and how an organization can use this information to cross-sell more products or services.

Customer churn—determining (predicting) which customers are likely to leave, and what tactics can help the firm avoid unwanted defections.

Collaborative filtering—personalizing an individual customer’s experience based on the trends and preferences identified across similar customers.

Fraud detection—uncovering (predicting) patterns consistent with criminal activity.

Hiring and promotion—identifying characteristics consistent with employee success in the firm’s various roles.

      Moore’s Law

      Moore’s prediction: The number of transistors on a microchip doubles every 18 months (at constant production costs per unit).

      Moore, Gordon (1965) Cramming more components onto integrated circuits, Electronics, Volume 38, Number 8, April 19, 1965; Intel Corp., intel.com/content/www/us/en/silicon-innovations/moores-law-technology.html

      INSY 2299 · Session 10
      Moore’s Law and More

      Two “laws” of technology: faster and cheaper computing

      Moore’s Law

      Processing power

      • Gordon Moore predicted in 1965: the number of transistors on a microchip doubles every 18 months // chip performance per dollar doubles every 18 months
      • Conclusion: computational costs increasingly less important; development time more important

      Kryder’s Law

      Storage power

      • Based on Mark Kryder: refers to the rapid increases in magnetic drive storage density during the last 60 years to today’s smaller, high-volume drives and was found to double every 12 months

      INSY 2299 · Session 10
      Moore’s Law and More

      Why should we care (at a business school)?

      Why is Moore’s Law important for accounting/operations? How does it influence managerial thinking?

      Hardware users

      Rapid temporal depreciation of computing equipment forces management to consider accounting and budgeting factors such as the useful life of the equipment, capital budget expenditures, and training budgets. Exemplary trade-off: rent vs. buy hardware (such as servers or software).

      Hardware sellers

      In addition, because the value of chips falls rapidly, excess chip-containing inventory can cost the company money. Dell claims its inventory depreciates as much as one percent per week. As a result, it becomes imperative to reduce inventory by just-in-time ordering and manufacturing processes.
